lead: A force that acts for a short time changes a particle's motion by an amount that depends on both the force and how long it acts. That product is impulse, measured in newton seconds (N·s). The impulse-momentum principle says the total impulse on a particle equals the change in its momentum. Engineers use it for cricket-ball hits, hammer blows, rocket thrust, car crashes and recoil, where the force is large, changes quickly and is hard to write as a simple function of time.
prereq: You need F = ma from 5.5 and resolving a vector into components from 5.2.

sections.h3: Impulse is area under the force-time graph

blocks.text: A constant force F acting for a time Δt gives an impulse I = F Δt. Real forces change during contact: a bat on a ball, a hammer on a nail, a car on a barrier. Divide the contact time into small intervals. On each interval the force is almost constant, so the impulse on that interval is F Δt. Adding the intervals gives I = ∫ F dt from t₁ to t₂. Impulse is a vector in N·s, pointing along the force.
I = ∫ F dt  (from t₁ to t₂)
blocks.where: I is linear impulse in N·s; F is the force in N at time t in s; t₁ and t₂ are the start and end of the contact in s.

blocks.text: On a force-time graph, impulse is the area under the curve. The peak force is not the average force. The average force over the contact is F_avg = I / Δt, where Δt = t₂ − t₁. It is the height of a rectangle that has the same area and the same base as the actual force-time curve. For a triangular pulse of peak F_max and base Δt, the area is ½ F_max Δt.

items: For components: I_x = ∫ F_x dt, and similarly for y and z.
The unit N·s equals kg·m/s, the unit of momentum.

blocks.text: Momentum is p = mv, with m in kg and v in m/s, so p is in kg·m/s. Newton's second law is F = ma = m dv/dt. Integrate both sides from time 1 to time 2: ∫F dt = m v₂ − m v₁. Rearranged, m v₁ + ∫F dt = m v₂. This is the impulse-momentum principle, also called the impulse-momentum theorem.
m v₁ + ∫ F dt = m v₂
blocks.where: m is mass in kg; v₁ and v₂ are initial and final velocities in m/s; ∫F dt is the total external impulse in N·s.

blocks.text: Use it component by component. In the x direction, m v₁ₓ + ∫Fₓ dt = m v₂ₓ. If the external impulse in a direction is zero, momentum in that direction does not change. Internal forces between parts of a system cancel in pairs. For a system of particles, ΣF_ext = d(Σmv)/dt. Recoil of a gun, an explosion, and a bullet embedding in a block all follow this rule along a line. The next chapter 5.8 adds how much speed is returned in a collision.

items: Choose a positive direction and mark it on a sketch.
Write every velocity with its sign in that direction.
Compute the total external impulse in that direction; if it is zero, use momentum conservation.
Solve for the unknown velocity or impulse, then check units.

sections.h3: Moment of momentum about a point

blocks.text: Moment of momentum about a point O, also called angular momentum, is H_O = r × m v. Here r is the position vector from O to the particle in m, m is mass in kg, and v is velocity in m/s. H_O is in kg·m²/s and is perpendicular to the plane of r and v by the right-hand rule. For plane motion its magnitude is m v d, where d is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of velocity; take anticlockwise as positive.
ΣM_O = dH_O / dt   and   ∫ M_O dt = H_O2 − H_O1
blocks.where: H_O is moment of momentum about O in kg·m²/s; ΣM_O is total moment about O in N·m; ∫M_O dt is angular impulse in N·m·s.

blocks.text: The first equation is the moment-of-momentum equation for a particle. The second defines angular impulse: the moment of a force integrated over time equals the change in moment of momentum. When the force is central—its line always passes through O—the moment about O is zero, so H_O stays constant. A satellite under gravity from the Earth and a ball tied to a string are examples. Conservation of angular momentum is the same statement with zero external moment.

figure.caption: The area under the triangular pulse is the impulse, 10.5 N·s. The peak force is 2100 N, but the average force over 0.01 s is 1050 N.

spec.aria: A triangular force-time pulse peaking at 2100 N; the area under it is the impulse of 10.5 N·s delivered to the ball.

examples.question: A cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg arrives at a bat at 30 m/s. The bat sends it straight back along the same line at 40 m/s. The bat is in contact with the ball for 0.01 s. Find (a) the impulse on the ball and (b) the average force exerted by the bat.
steps: Take the outgoing direction, away from the bat, as positive. Then the initial velocity v₁ = −30 m/s and the final velocity v₂ = +40 m/s.
Initial momentum p₁ = m v₁ = 0.15 × (−30) = −4.5 kg·m/s.
Final momentum p₂ = m v₂ = 0.15 × 40 = +6.0 kg·m/s.
Impulse I = p₂ − p₁ = 6.0 − (−4.5) = 10.5 N·s. The positive sign means the impulse is outgoing.
Average force F_avg = I / Δt = 10.5 / 0.01 = 1050 N, acting outgoing.
examples.answer: The impulse on the ball is 10.5 N·s outgoing, and the average force is 1050 N outgoing.
examples.check:
m = 0.15
v1 = -30
v2 = 40
dt = 0.01
p1 = m * v1
p2 = m * v2
I = p2 - p1
F_avg = I / dt
print(I)
print(F_avg)

traps: Signs: a ball hit straight back has a change of velocity equal to the sum of the speeds, not the difference. Choose a positive direction and keep it.
Impulse is the whole area under the force-time graph, not peak force times time. For a triangle use ½ × base × height.
Impulse and momentum have the same units, N·s = kg·m/s. Do not report impulse in N or in joules.
Momentum is conserved in a direction only when the external impulse in that direction is zero. Internal forces cancel, but friction, gravity or a wall can change momentum.
Average force is impulse divided by contact time, not the peak force. For a triangular pulse the peak is twice the average force.

quiz.q: Define linear impulse and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: Linear impulse is I = ∫F dt, the force integrated over the time it acts. It is a vector in N·s, along the force.

quiz.q: Explain why a small force acting for a long time can give the same impulse as a large force acting for a short time.
quiz.a: Impulse is the area under the force-time graph, not just the height. If the two areas are equal, the impulses are equal even when the peak forces differ.

quiz.q: A 0.2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s is stopped in 0.02 s. Find the impulse on the ball and the average force, taking the initial motion as positive.
quiz.a: v₁ = +5 m/s, v₂ = 0. I = m(v₂ − v₁) = 0.2 × (0 − 5) = −1 N·s. F_avg = I / Δt = −1 / 0.02 = −50 N. The negative sign means impulse and force point opposite to the initial motion.

quiz.q: A bullet embeds in a wooden block resting on a smooth floor. Explain why momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.
quiz.a: There is no external horizontal impulse on the bullet-block system, so total horizontal momentum is conserved. Internal forces between bullet and block are equal and opposite. Kinetic energy is lost to heat, sound and permanent deformation of the wood.

quiz.q: A force-time graph is a triangle with peak force 600 N and base 0.05 s. Find the impulse and the average force.
quiz.a: Area of triangle = ½ × 600 × 0.05 = 15 N·s. F_avg = 15 / 0.05 = 300 N.

quiz.q: A satellite moves under the central gravitational force of the Earth. Why is its angular momentum about the Earth constant?
quiz.a: The force always points along the line joining the satellite to the Earth, so its moment about the Earth is zero. Therefore dH_O/dt = 0 and H_O is constant.

quiz.q: State the moment-of-momentum equation for a particle about a fixed point O.
quiz.a: ΣM_O = dH_O/dt, where ΣM_O is the total moment about O and H_O = r × mv is the moment of momentum about O.

quiz.q: A 0.1 kg particle has position r = (2i + 3j) m and velocity v = (4i) m/s. Find its moment of momentum about the origin.
quiz.a: H_O = r × m v = 0.1 × [(2i + 3j) × 4i] = 0.1 × (12)(j × i) = 0.1 × (−12k) = −1.2k kg·m²/s. The magnitude is 1.2 kg·m²/s, clockwise in the xy plane.

beyond: Not for the exam. Rocket engineers use the same impulse idea with variable mass and write the rocket equation; search for specific impulse and thrust curve. Crash-test engineers measure force-time pulses to design airbags and crumple zones. Sports engineers use bat and ball impulse data to tune equipment. Satellite attitude control uses conservation of angular momentum with reaction wheels. Search next for impulse response and the rocket equation.
